newsitem.title: USA: Treasurer in Chicago indicted for ghost payroll.
newsitem.headline: Treasurer in Chicago indicted for ghost payroll.

text.p: Two Illinois state legislators, the Cook County treasurer and his deputy have been indicted in an alleged no-show job scheme that netted the lawmakers thousands of dollars in return for political favours, prosecutors said Tuesday.

Treasurer Edward Rosewell, 70, and his deputy, James Fuglsang, 51, allegedly hid State Senator Bruce Farley, 54, and State Representative Miguel Santiago, 44, on the office payroll, paying them $320,000 in salary and benefits from 1990 to 1995.

"These arrangements were made ... for political favours and other reasons," James Burns, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, told a news conference. "This is a tragic day to see these four individuals indicted."

According to Burns, when Rosewell's political opponent demanded to see payroll records before the 1994 election, he and his cronies allegedly put the ghost payrollers on temporary leave and invented the title of "legislative liaison" for them.
A grand jury subpoena in 1995 finally halted the practice, he said, but the conspiracy to hide the scheme continued.

Rosewell was indicted on 17 counts, including aiding and abetting theft, conspiracy to commit theft, mail fraud and obstruction of justice. The counts carried maximum prison terms of five or 10 years, $250,000 fines, and possible restitution. Fuglsang was indicted on 18 counts, Farley on nine counts and Santiago on seven counts.
Rosewell is the longest-serving elected official in the county with 23 years in his post.
His office, which is responsible for collecting county property taxes, was recently under fire for millions of dollars in revenue shortfalls, which Rosewell blamed on an accounting problem.
Federal prosecutors also have an ongoing investigation of ghost payrolling in city hall involving several aldermen.
